fixes.explanation: That's it, friend. The writer says, "Make clear to me the way of Your precepts; then I will meditate on Your wonders." (Psalm 119:27) First the way gets clear, then he meditates on God's wonders. Understanding leads him to wonder.

Doorposts do show up in Deuteronomy 6:9, but not in this verse. The writer says, "Make clear to me the way of Your precepts; then I will meditate on Your wonders." (Psalm 119:27) What he promises is to meditate on God's wonders.

I like where your head's at, friend, but this verse never mentions children. The writer says, "Make clear to me the way of Your precepts; then I will meditate on Your wonders." (Psalm 119:27) Watch the order: the way gets clear first, and then comes the meditating. His promise is to meditate on God's wonders.

Forgiveness is a fine prayer, but it's not the one he prays here. The writer says, "My soul melts with sorrow; strengthen me according to Your word." (Psalm 119:28) Melting is his word for himself, and the ask that follows is strengthen. I'd ask for the same if I felt like a cookie left on the stove.

Wisdom is a fine road, friend, but he's not pointing to it on this map. The writer says, "I have chosen the way of truth; I have set Your ordinances before me." (Psalm 119:30) Right after the path of deceit, the road he names is the way of truth.
That's right, friend. The writer says, "I have set Your ordinances before me." (Psalm 119:30) Before him, not behind him. He sets God's ordinances in front of him.

Not this time, friend. The writer says, "I cling to Your testimonies, O LORD; let me not be put to shame." (Psalm 119:31) So yes, he asks the LORD not to let him be put to shame. I picture someone hanging on to the counter edge with both hands while praying it.

That's it, baker. The writer says, "I run in the path of Your commandments, for You will enlarge my heart." (Psalm 119:32) The reason is what God will do for him. He runs because God will enlarge his heart.

Good guess, but that's not the reason this verse gives. The writer says, "I run in the path of Your commandments, for You will enlarge my heart." (Psalm 119:32) His reason is that God will enlarge his heart. Enemies aren't the reason he names.

Sundown would make a dramatic reason, friend, but the verse doesn't give it. The writer says, "I run in the path of Your commandments, for You will enlarge my heart." (Psalm 119:32) The reason he gives is that God will enlarge his heart. No stopwatch needed.

Foreign gods would be a big thing to steer clear of, friend, but he doesn't name them in this verse. The writer says, "Turn my heart to Your testimonies and not to covetous gain." (Psalm 119:36) What he asks God to turn his heart away from is covetous gain. He asks God to do the turning.

Proud rulers would make a dramatic answer, baker, but they're not in this verse. The writer says, "Turn my heart to Your testimonies and not to covetous gain." (Psalm 119:36) The thing he doesn't want his heart turned toward is covetous gain. Notice he points at his own heart, not at anybody else.

Yes, baker. The writer says, "Establish Your word to Your servant, to produce reverence for You." (Psalm 119:38) He asks God to establish His word to him. Reverence for God is what he wants that word to produce.

Sacrifices would be a big word to pick, baker, but it's not what this verse says. The writer says, "Establish Your word to Your servant, to produce reverence for You." (Psalm 119:38) The word that fits is reverence. He's asking for it to be produced for God.

Songs is a fun guess, friend, but that's not the word here. The writer says, "Establish Your word to Your servant, to produce reverence for You." (Psalm 119:38) The word is reverence. That's what he asks God's word to produce.

He doesn't say that, baker. The writer says, "Turn away the disgrace I dread, for Your judgments are good." (Psalm 119:39) The reason he gives is about God: God's judgments are good. He doesn't mention his own record.

Rest sounds nice, friend, and I'd take a nap right now myself, but that's not what this verse says. The writer says, "Then I can answer him who taunts, for I trust in Your word." (Psalm 119:42) What he says he'll be able to do is answer the one who taunts.

Rebuilding walls is in Nehemiah 2:17, but not in this verse. The writer says, "Then I can answer him who taunts, for I trust in Your word." (Psalm 119:42) He says he can answer the one who taunts him.
Right, friend. The writer says, "Then I can answer him who taunts, for I trust in Your word." (Psalm 119:42) The trust he names is in God's word. His own strength isn't mentioned.
His soul melting with sorrow does show up in Psalm 119:28, but sorrow isn't the word here. He says, "And I will walk in freedom, for I have sought Your precepts." (Psalm 119:45) The word is freedom.

Yes, baker. The writer says, "I will speak of Your testimonies before kings, and I will not be ashamed." (Psalm 119:46) He says he will speak before kings, and he says he will not be ashamed. That's a bold line.

Not this time, friend. The writer says, "I will speak of Your testimonies before kings, and I will not be ashamed." (Psalm 119:46) So he says he will not be ashamed, even speaking before kings. I think that's a brave thing to say out loud.

Studying is a fine habit, friend, but he doesn't say it here. The writer says, "I delight in Your commandments because I love them." (Psalm 119:47) Love is the reason he gives for his delight, not a study plan.
